title: South-east Australia's post-1997 runoff loss removed more baseflow than an effective-rainfall loss predicts; the eastern US loss did not (daily flow, 185 + 281 catchments, 1951-2025)
abstract: Question: south-east Australian and eastern US catchments both lost runoff per unit rain after 1997, but only the Australian loss started in a drought and stayed as a persistent low-runoff state. Do the two losses have the same hydrograph fingerprint? Approach: we used daily flow for 185 south-east Australian catchments (CAMELS-AUS v2.03, 1951-2021) and 550 US CAMELS catchments (USGS NWIS, water years 1951-2025). We separated baseflow with the Lyne-Hollick filter. For each flow metric we fitted a 1951-1996 relation to annual rain, previous-year rain and temperature. From the calibrated rain slopes we calculated the fingerprint of an effective-rainfall loss (rain lost before it reaches the flow stores) of the same total size. We wrote the plan before we calculated any component result. Results: in the eastern US, the observed residuals agreed with this fingerprint for baseflow, quickflow, baseflow index (BFI excess -0.02 SD, 95% CI -0.15 to +0.11) and no-flow days. In south-east Australia, an effective-rainfall loss predicts a higher BFI, but BFI fell: the excess was -0.37 SD (-0.58 to -0.20) after 2009 and -0.40 in 1997-2009, against +0.11 in a 1981-1996 stationarity check. No-flow days increased more than predicted (+0.79 SD). In wet years after 2009, Australian baseflow stayed -1.33 SD low and quickflow -0.80 SD. The BFI excess was the same with SILO rain, which halves the total deficit. The signature was strongest in intermittent Australian streams and had a small link to deficit persistence. Limitations: the planned baseflow and low-flow-quantile rule was not met; most supporting tests are post hoc; baseflow is a filter output; Australian flow ends in 2021; the cause of the storage loss was not identified.
